column2: A sampling distribution shows:
column3: The distribution of a statistic from ALL possible samples of the same size
column4: The distribution of individual values in one sample
column5: The distribution of the entire population
column6: The shape of any random variable

column2: Why is it usually impossible to construct an ACTUAL sampling distribution?
column3: There are far too many possible samples to collect them all
column4: Sampling distributions don't actually exist in real life
column5: You would need to know the population mean first
column6: It requires expensive equipment

column2: If we can't get all possible samples, how can we study sampling distributions?
column3: We can SIMULATE them by taking many random samples from the population
column4: We just guess what they look like
column5: We ignore them and use the population instead
column6: We only use samples of size 1

column2: The Central Limit Theorem says that when sample size is large enough, the sampling distribution of the mean will be:
column3: Approximately normal, regardless of the population's shape
column4: Exactly the same shape as the population
column5: Skewed in the opposite direction of the population
column6: Impossible to predict

column2: What makes the Central Limit Theorem 'amazing' according to statisticians?
column3: It works no matter what the population distribution looks like
column4: It requires very small sample sizes to work
column5: It only applies to normal populations
column6: It gives exact answers instead of approximations

column2: A population is strongly skewed right. For the sampling distribution of the mean to be approximately normal, you need:
column3: A sufficiently large sample size
column4: The population to first become normal
column5: A sample size of exactly 30
column6: To remove all outliers from the population

column2: If a population is already normally distributed, the sampling distribution of the mean will be:
column3: Approximately normal, even with small sample sizes
column4: Skewed for small samples, normal for large samples
column5: Unpredictable regardless of sample size
column6: Uniform instead of normal

column2: As sample size INCREASES, the standard deviation of the sampling distribution:
column3: Decreases — sample means cluster more tightly around the population mean
column4: Increases — more data means more variability
column5: Stays the same — it only depends on the population
column6: Becomes unpredictable

column2: Compared to n = 5, a sampling distribution with n = 50 would be:
column3: Narrower (less spread) and more likely to be approximately normal
column4: Wider (more spread) and more skewed
column5: Exactly the same shape and spread
column6: Impossible to compare without more information

column2: A population has a bimodal (two-peaked) distribution. With n = 2, the sampling distribution will probably be:
column3: NOT approximately normal — small samples from non-normal populations stay non-normal
column4: Perfectly normal — the CLT always works
column5: Exactly bimodal like the population
column6: Uniform

column2: That same bimodal population with n = 100 would have a sampling distribution that is:
column3: Approximately normal — large samples make CLT work even for unusual populations
column4: Still bimodal, just narrower
column5: Impossible to describe
column6: Skewed right

column2: For CLT to apply, the sample values must be:
column3: Independent of each other
column4: Exactly normally distributed
column5: All positive numbers
column6: Collected at the same time

column2: A randomization distribution is created by:
column3: Repeatedly reassigning response values to treatment groups at random
column4: Taking many samples from the same population
column5: Calculating the mean of one sample many times
column6: Measuring the same subjects repeatedly

column2: The purpose of a randomization distribution is to show:
column3: What results would look like if there were NO real treatment effect (chance alone)
column4: The exact effect of the treatment
column5: How the population is distributed
column6: Whether the sample size was large enough

column2: When creating a randomization distribution, we ignore the original group assignments because:
column3: We want to model what happens when group assignment doesn't matter (no effect)
column4: The original assignments were probably wrong
column5: Random assignment always produces the same results
column6: We need to increase the sample size

column2: In a randomization test, if the observed result falls in the TAIL of the distribution, this suggests:
column3: The result is unlikely to have occurred by chance alone — evidence of a real effect
column4: The result is exactly what we'd expect by chance
column5: The experiment was conducted incorrectly
column6: The sample size was too small

column2: A randomization distribution produces a probability of 0.03 for the observed result. This means:
column3: Only 3% of random reassignments produced a result this extreme — unlikely by chance
column4: The treatment worked exactly 3% of the time
column5: We need 3% more data to draw conclusions
column6: The experiment had a 3% error rate

column2: If a randomization test gives a probability of 0.45, what should you conclude?
column3: The observed result could easily have occurred by chance — weak/no evidence of effect
column4: The treatment definitely works
column5: The treatment definitely doesn't work
column6: The experiment needs to be repeated exactly 0.45 times

column2: A small probability from a randomization test (like 0.01) provides:
column3: Evidence that the observed effect is real, not just due to chance
column4: Proof that the treatment works perfectly
column5: Evidence that the experiment was flawed
column6: No useful information

column2: What does 'by chance alone' mean in the context of randomization?
column3: The result that would occur if treatment had NO effect and group differences were just random
column4: The probability that we made a calculation error
column5: The likelihood of getting exactly the population parameter
column6: The chance that our sample is biased

column2: A randomization distribution is centered at 0 (no difference). If your observed difference is far from 0, this suggests:
column3: Your result is unusual if there's truly no effect — possible evidence the treatment works
column4: Your calculation was wrong
column5: The randomization was done incorrectly
column6: You need a larger sample

column2: How many simulations are typically used to build a randomization distribution?
column3: Hundreds or thousands (e.g., 1,000 or 10,000)
column4: Exactly 30
column5: Just 2 or 3
column6: The same as the sample size

column2: Each point in a randomization distribution represents:
column3: One possible outcome if groups were randomly assigned with no real treatment effect
column4: One person in the original sample
column5: One measurement from the population
column6: The mean of the entire population

column2: A researcher observes a difference of 5 units between treatment and control. The randomization distribution shows this is larger than 98% of simulated differences. The probability is:
column3: 0.02 — only 2% of chance results were this extreme
column4: 0.98 — most results were smaller
column5: 0.50 — it's right in the middle
column6: 5.00 — same as the observed difference

column2: Why is the shape of a randomization distribution often approximately normal?
column3: The Central Limit Theorem applies to differences in means too
column4: All randomization distributions are required to be normal
column5: We force it to be normal by our choice of simulations
column6: Random chance always produces bell curves

column2: A sampling distribution helps us understand _____, while a randomization distribution helps us assess _____.
column3: How statistics vary across samples; whether an observed effect could be due to chance
column4: Population parameters; sample statistics
column5: Individual values; group means
column6: Probability; frequency

column3: We can see the pattern that emerges from many samples without collecting them all in real life
column4: Simulations are always more accurate than real data
column5: Real sampling is illegal in most countries

column4: Population shape — skewed populations have more spread
column5: The number of simulations run
column6: Whether we use replacement when sampling

column3: Larger samples give means that are closer to the true population mean

column5: The population got smaller

column5: How many more subjects do we need?
